KEY MESSAGE 1: Heat and humidity will peak today.

Increasingly southwesterly flow at the surface and aloft will 
carry warm and humid air into the region today, well in advance
of a cold front moving southeast across the Upper Great Lakes. 

A gradually narrowing SW-NE axis of very high PWAT air (1.8 - 2
inches) will reach the south shore of Lake Erie during the early
afternoon, then sag SE across the NW Mtns early this evening
before reaching the Southern Tier of PA before daybreak
Thursday. This will be a 0.5 to 0.75 inch increase in PWAT over
the upcoming 15 hours which will make it feel much more
uncomfortably humid later today and much of tonight.

The late day/nighttime peak in the won't result in high heat
indices today with apparent temps only about 3-4 deg F higher
than the actual temps.  

High temperatures will be around 2 to 4 degrees warmer than 
they were today, generally ranging from the low to mid 80s. Heat
index values may touch the 90F mark in the south central 
mountains on Wednesday as dewpoints climb back into the mid to 
upper 60s. Rain-free conditions will prevail for much of the 
day, though we should start to see thunderstorms develop over 
northwest PA by the evening.

--------------------------------------------------------------

KEY MESSAGE 2: Showers and scattered strong to potentially severe
thunderstorms, with the threat for localized gusty to damaging
winds for late today and early tonight, mainly across the NW
third of PA.

Surface low pressure system will be moving across northern 
Ontario with a cold front extending south/southwest through the
Great Lakes and Ohio Valley. 

Tightening llvl pressure gradient will lead to an increase in 
synoptic scale/gradient winds this afternoon into Thursday. 

Wind gusts will increase in into the 20s today on the hilltops 
and also across the Lower SUsquehanna Valley. A gust near 30MPH
is possible on the tops of the Laurels Wed night just before 
the front. 

The cold front will provide enough lift of the airmass,
(containing a high shear/relatively low instability environment)
to create numerous showers and scattered, embedded thunderstorms,
with the majority of this convection occurring before the front
passes later tonight in the north and Thursday morning in the 
south. 

There is some potential for severe weather across northwest PA 
with these storms as confidence in favorable overlap of CAPE and
shear continues to increase with SPC maintaining similar
areal coverage of their slight risk of severe weather. Most 
guidance (including the latest HREF) shows  500 to 1200 J/kg of
MUCAPE developing out ahead of the front, with the highest 
values concentrated over our northwestern counties. 

Coinciding with this will be an increase in 0-6 km westerly 
bulk shear, with values between 40 to 50 knots. This should 
support some fast-moving discrete cells, growing upscale into
some line segments containing mini bows with an enhanced threat
for wind damage late today/this evening from Warren to Bradford
and points about 40 NM to the South.

Model soundings do show some turning in the lowest 0-3 km in 
association with a 40 to 45 knot low-level jet, and a few 
transient supercell structures or circulations embedded in 
linear segments cannot be ruled out. SPC has included a 2% 
tornado contour that covers much of the slight risk area.

Showers and thunderstorms should weaken as they move south and
east through the night into a more stable airmass. However, 
they will still be capable of producing localized heavy 
downpours. 

The current WPC outlook for Thurs paints a SLGT risk of 
excessive rainfall over portions of Cambria and Somerset 
Counties. Some CAMs show the potential for up to an inch of rain
to fall into Thursday morning in the slight risk area, though 
most guidance would suggest that up to half of an inch of rain 
is the more likely outcome. Even though flash flood guidance is 
relatively low in these areas, the potential for any flash 
flooding appears to be low at this time unless any areas see 
training thunderstorms develop.

High pressure builds behind the cold front, giving way to a dry
and sunny Friday. 

Low level moisture lurking just south of the Mason/Dixon line
Fri/Fri night will advance NE across the state on Saturday as
SFC high pressure moves well off the Mid Atlantic and Southern
New England Coast. 

This will lead to some showers spreading NE across the region
with a few PM TSRA possible Saturday and/or Sunday afternoons, 
especially over the western mtns. A more- active (wetter) 
pattern is in store for Mon-Tues. But, the flat upper ridge over
the southern half of the CONUS will make it difficult for deep 
moisture to make it into PA ahead of any shots of atmos forcing.
The second half of the week probably ends dry as the upper 
ridge pumps up over the central CONUS.
